title: The Bosphorus Brief — 23 September 2026
overview: A school shooting in Turkey and a fresh wave of citizenship revocations lead today's news, alongside a weaker lira and steady disinflation signals from the central bank. Regionally, UN-sidelines diplomacy on Iran continues, with Ankara staying visible on Black Sea and Gulf security matters.

sections.heading: School Shooting Prompts Safety Questions
sections.body: At least 11 people were wounded in a shooting outside a high school in Turkey, an incident covered by both Turkish and international outlets including CNN, Hürriyet Daily News, and The New York Times. Details on the cause remain limited in the material available. For families with children in Turkish schools, this is worth watching for official statements on campus security measures in the coming days, though there is no indication of a broader pattern or ongoing threat.

sections.heading: Citizenship Revocations Widen
sections.body: Turkish authorities have canceled or withdrawn citizenship for 6,134 people over fraud or security concerns, with a further 1,070 cases identified in what's being called a second wave tied to citizenship-by-investment scrutiny. If you or someone you know obtained Turkish citizenship through investment programs, this is a good moment to ensure paperwork is in order and consult a lawyer if there's any uncertainty about how the case was processed — reporting suggests authorities are focused on fraudulent applications rather than legitimate ones, but the scale of the review is significant.

sections.heading: Lira Slips, Central Bank Stays the Course
sections.body: USD/TRY sits at 48.82 today, with the lira hitting fresh record lows against major currencies. Despite this, Turkey's central bank says disinflation is continuing even amid supply-side pressures — a signal that policymakers see current price trends as manageable rather than alarming. For residents managing budgets in lira, this means continued attention to exchange rates when planning larger purchases or transfers, but no signal of policy panic from Ankara.

sections.heading: Rights Groups Flag Escalating Pressures
sections.body: Amnesty International describes an escalating rights crisis affecting LGBTI groups and activists in Turkey, while separate reporting notes a jailed pastor in Turkey has been appointed by the US to a religious freedom commission. These developments sit alongside Algeria's detention of Christians facing charges and broader religious-freedom advocacy stories from China. None of this points to acute new risk for residents, but it's part of a pattern worth watching for anyone involved in advocacy, faith communities, or civil society work in the region.

sections.heading: Diplomacy on the Sidelines
sections.body: Trump described a 'very good' three-hour US-Iran meeting at the UN, even as he separately warned Iran needs to act fast. The Kremlin confirmed Erdoğan raised a Black Sea proposal in a 90-minute meeting with Putin — a reminder that Ankara continues to position itself as a facilitator on regional security issues. Turkey also joined Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Egypt in affirming Riyadh's right to self-defense, and signed a $2 million grant deal with the US on small nuclear reactors.

closing: Stay safe out there, and take care of the paperwork before the çay gets cold.
